prime.problem: Clients of the image service need to know which of the 40 resize servers are running right now. DNS only knows what could be at an address, caches it for minutes and never notices a crash. With servers joining, dying and pausing all the time, clients keep sending work to dead machines.
prime.fits: Builds on the request-path card's DNS and load balancer, and on the end-to-end card's 20 s ZooKeeper timeout. The registry itself is a replicated majority-quorum store, which the Raft card later explains from the inside.
expect: ephemeral nodes tied to a session
what ZooKeeper is not (cache, pub-sub, monitor)
prime.goal: Trace how a registry learns a server died (and falsely decides a paused one did), compute what the detection delay costs in misdirected requests, and size a registry ensemble by the crashes it must survive.

attend: Why does nobody have to delete srv-2's entry after it crashes?
Why was srv-3 removed at t = 49 even though its process never died, and what does it have to do when it wakes?
What sets the number of requests sent to a dead server, and why is a DNS TTL so much worse?
Why does a 4-node ensemble survive no more crashes than a 3-node one?
How can a GC pause on a registry member contribute to quorum loss?

must: Each server registers an ephemeral node tied to its session → the session lives while heartbeats arrive → silence past the timeout (20 s) ends the session and deletes the node → watchers are told → the list cleans itself

Detection is a timeout → a crashed server keeps receiving traffic until it expires → 20 s × 250 req/s = 5,000 misdirected requests (vs 75,000 at a 300 s DNS TTL) → the timeout is "the major cost for MTTR"

A long GC pause is silence too → the session expires while the process is alive (srv-3 at t = 49) → when it wakes its heartbeat is rejected and it must re-register → a registry can't tell paused from dead

The registry must not be a single point of failure → replicate it and commit on a majority q = ⌊n/2⌋ + 1 → any two majorities share a server, so they can't disagree → n = 3 survives 1 crash, n = 5 survives 2, even n buys nothing
elevated: Watches are one-shot notifications → clients don't poll → the registry's load stays small even with many clients, which is why it can keep all state in memory (node data capped around 1 MB)

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the registry timeline for one crashed and one paused server, then write the quorum formula and the table row for n = 3 and n = 5. One sentence each on why DNS and a database table fall short.
checklist: ephemeral node + session + heartbeats: entries expire with their owner
detection delay = session timeout → 5,000 requests to a dead server at 20 s
a GC pause looks like a crash: false expiry, re-register on wake
majority quorum: 2 of 3 survives 1, 3 of 5 survives 2; even n wastes a machine
DNS: cached, never notices crashes; DB table: polling, no ephemeral entries

retrieve.q: Explain why ephemeral nodes plus watches answer "who is up right now?" better than a database table the servers write to.
answer: an ephemeral entry disappears on its own when the owner's session ends; a table row stays until someone deletes it
watches push each change; a table must be polled, adding load
the registry orders its change notifications; a table gives no such guarantee

retrieve.q: Walk through the registry timeline for srv-3 from t = 29 to t = 55: what the registry sees, what the client's list shows, and what srv-3 does when it wakes.
answer: t = 29: last heartbeat; t = 30 the GC pause starts
t = 49: 20 s of silence, session expires, node deleted, watch fires: list becomes [srv-1]
t = 55: srv-3 wakes; its heartbeat is rejected (session gone)
it opens a new session and re-registers: list back to [srv-1, srv-3]

retrieve.q: Your three-node registry lost writes during an incident where one member crashed and another hit a long GC pause. Should you go to 4 nodes or 5, and why?
answer: n = 3 needs 2; crashed + paused leaves 1 < 2, so writes stop
4 nodes needs 3 and still survives only 1 failure: no gain
5 nodes needs 3 and survives 2: the incident's crash + pause leaves 3, writes continue

compare.q: This card uses a majority quorum from the outside; the Raft card builds one. What does Raft add on top of "commit when a majority agrees" to make the overlap argument actually work?
answer: one leader per term that orders every write into one log
a vote restriction: only a candidate whose log has every committed entry can win
together with overlapping majorities, a new leader always holds every committed write

compare.q: A registry tells clients which servers exist; a message broker hands work to whichever consumer is free. When would you route resize jobs through a queue instead of having clients pick servers from the registry?
answer: a queue decouples producers from consumer health: a dead consumer just stops taking jobs
registry-based client balancing sends work straight to a server, so a stale list means misdirected requests until expiry
use a queue for expensive, independent jobs (the resize case); a registry for request/response calls and for membership and config

predict.q: You change the session timeout from 20 s to 30 s. How many requests now go to a crashed server at 250 requests/s, and does srv-3's 25 s GC pause still get it removed? Commit first.
predict.answer: 30 × 250 = 7,500 requests go to a crashed server before its entry vanishes (up from 5,000). But srv-3's 25 s pause no longer outlasts the timeout, so its session survives and it's never falsely removed. The timeout trades detection speed (MTTR) against false deaths, exactly the delay card's too-short vs too-long dilemma. At 10 s: 2,500 requests, and far more pauses become false deaths.

apply.task: Modify simulate() in code/service-discovery.py to take the timeout as a parameter, and run it at 10 s, 20 s and 30 s. For each, record when srv-2 is removed, whether srv-3 is falsely removed, and the misdirected requests at 250 req/s. Then use quorum(n) to say whether a 5-node ensemble keeps accepting writes with one member crashed and one paused.
apply.done: Your table shows srv-2 removed at t = 15, 25 and 35; srv-3 falsely removed at 10 s and 20 s but not at 30 s; 2,500, 5,000 and 7,500 misdirected requests; and n = 5 with 2 down keeps 3 = q, so writes continue.
apply.hint: srv-2's last heartbeat is at t = 5, so removal is at 5 + timeout. srv-3's pause is 25 s; a timeout at or below 25 s expires it.
